Chapter 7: The Art of Staying Grounded.
There’s a strange paradox in spaceflight. The farther you travel from Earth, the more you realize just how deeply you belong to it.
For so many astronauts, orbiting the planet brings this fresh sense of connection—not just to home, but to all the people and places left behind.
Staying grounded—emotionally, mentally, spiritually—suddenly becomes essential.
Picture this: after a long day packed with experiments and repairs, you finally get a quiet moment. The work is finished. Outside your window, there’s just a swirl of blue and white—Earth, breathtaking and distant.
And in that silence, you start to long for the familiar. Maybe it’s the sound of rain, or the smell of grass, or just the laughter of people you love. Even with your crew close by, it can feel lonely up there.
So, what do you do? One crew member, missing home, begins a ritual. Every night, they write a short note to their family, sharing the day’s tiny victories and frustrations. Someone else finds comfort in music, playing a favorite song before bed.
It’s these small acts that become anchors—reminders of life beyond the station. They help you keep perspective, even when the world feels impossibly far away.
Here’s something to pay attention to: Staying grounded doesn’t mean ignoring the challenges, or pretending you don’t miss home. It’s about finding ways to stay connected, to remember what truly matters, and carrying those connections into your work.
Most people don’t realize just how much strength comes from these little rituals, or how much they matter when everything else feels uncertain.
And you know what? This lesson holds true even back on Earth. In times of stress or chaos, it’s the simple routines—like your morning coffee, a walk in the park, or a quick call to a friend—that help keep you steady.
The world might feel overwhelming, but these small grounding acts remind us who we are, and what we’re working toward.
